power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: A 1-month lag in rainfall was associated with a statistically significant increase in dengue incidence (IRR = 1.008, 95% CI: 1.003-1.012, p = 0.002), corresponding to a 0.8% increase in expected case counts per unit (mm) increase in rainfall one month prior.

A 1-month lag in rainfall was associated with a statistically significant increase in dengue incidence (IRR = 1.008, 95% CI: 1.003-1.012, p = 0.002), corresponding to a 0.8% increase in expected case counts per unit (mm) increase in rainfall one month prior.

A 2-month rainfall lag showed a similar, slightly smaller effect (IRR = 1.006, 95% CI: 1.001-1.011, p = 0.027), indicating that elevated rainfall continues to predict higher case counts up to two months later, consistent with the time needed for standing water to support mosquito breeding and larval development.

Temperature lagged by 2 months showed a coefficient in the opposite direction from expectation (IRR = 0.965, 95% CI: 0.874-1.067, p = 0.436), and temperature lagged by 3 months showed a near-null effect (IRR = 0.986, 95% CI: 0.902-1.078, p = 0.736).

Temperature lagged by 2 months showed a coefficient in the opposite direction from expectation (IRR = 0.965, 95% CI: 0.874-1.067, p = 0.436), and temperature lagged by 3 months showed a near-null effect (IRR = 0.986, 95% CI: 0.902-1.078, p = 0.736).

A 1 mm increase in rainfall one month prior was associated with a 0.68% increase in expected monthly cases (IRR = 1.007, 95% CI: 1.003-1.011, p = 0.001), and a 1 mm increase two months prior with a 0.61% increase (IRR = 1.006, 95% CI: 1.002-1.011, p = 0.016).

A 1 mm increase in rainfall one month prior was associated with a 0.68% increase in expected monthly cases (IRR = 1.007, 95% CI: 1.003-1.011, p = 0.001), and a 1 mm increase two months prior with a 0.61% increase (IRR = 1.006, 95% CI: 1.002-1.011, p = 0.016).
Temperature at 2-and 3-month lag showed no significant association with case counts (temp lag-2: IRR = 0.977, 95% CI: 0.903-1.056, p = 0.549; temp lag-3: IRR = 0.973, 95% CI: 0.909-1.041, p = 0.417).
Temperature at 2-and 3-month lag showed no significant association with case counts (temp lag-2: IRR = 0.977, 95% CI: 0.903-1.056, p = 0.549; temp lag-3: IRR = 0.973, 95% CI: 0.909-1.041, p = 0.417).
A significant negative linear time trend was also detected (β = -0.0093, p = 0.026), indicating a decline in monthly case counts over the study period independent of season and climate.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.01", Text = "The GAM explained a substantially larger share of deviance in-sample (89.2%) than the best linear GLM (83.3%; Table 1), driven primarily by non-linear rainfall terms: the effective degrees of freedom (edf) for rainfall at 1-and 2-month lag were 2.57 and 2.31, respectively (both p < 0.01), indicating genuine curvature rather than a linear dose-response relationship."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.436", "p = 0.736", "p = 0.549", "p = 0.417", "p = 0.848 ", "p = 0.742"), Sentence = c("Temperature lagged by 2 months showed a coefficient in the opposite direction from expectation (IRR = 0.965, 95% CI: 0.874-1.067, p = 0.436), and temperature lagged by 3 months showed a near-null effect (IRR = 0.986, 95% CI: 0.902-1.078, p = 0.736).", "Temperature lagged by 2 months showed a coefficient in the opposite direction from expectation (IRR = 0.965, 95% CI: 0.874-1.067, p = 0.436), and temperature lagged by 3 months showed a near-null effect (IRR = 0.986, 95% CI: 0.902-1.078, p = 0.736).", "Temperature at 2-and 3-month lag showed no significant association with case counts (temp lag-2: IRR = 0.977, 95% CI: 0.903-1.056, p = 0.549;
